scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Vasoorimala originated as an Upa Devata (sub-deity) worshiped in temple complexes across Kerala and the Kodagu region of Karnataka.
The performance of Vasoorimala Theyyam emerged historically when smallpox epidemics broke out in the region.
Faced with fatal contagion, communities began worshiping the disease in the physical form of a Theyyam to alleviate suffering and rid themselves of pestilence.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Vasoorimala is venerated as a deity who controls and prevents infectious diseases, specifically smallpox, chickenpox, and measles.
The Theyyam is performed during temple rituals specifically for the cure of diseases and communal protection.
Its meaning is anchored in the cultural belief that deities responsible for sowing pestilence must be propitiated to grant healing.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The folklore and mythological origins of Vasoorimala are preserved in the literary work Aithihyamala, authored by Kottarathil Sankunni.
In mythic history, she is identified with Manodari, the wife of the Asura Darikan (or Darukan), who clashed with goddess Bhadrakali.
The deity is venerated across Kerala and extends into the Kodagu region of Karnataka.
Vasoorimala Theyyam forms part of the broader Theyyam ritual tradition of North Kerala, functioning within sacred lineages linked to Bhadrakali and Shiva worship.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Vasoorimala Theyyam is a sacred ritual embodiment of a Hindu deity conducted in temple precincts for the healing of communicable diseases. It is not an open social or performance dance and should not be casually imitated or treated as recreational entertainment.
